title: What Hitler Really Thought About Americans
hook: I thought America was a cartoon with a flag.

levels.name: The File
beats: A cowboy. A chewing-gum smile. A song on the radio that would not sit still. That was page one. Stay. I am going to tell you the sentence I got wrong.
I did not hate you. Hate is for a rival who can ruin your sleep. I slept fine. You were a store. A store with fireworks. A store that clapped at itself.
You know my name because it is easy to say like a curse. I knew your type because it was easy to put in a cartoon. I put you in a cartoon. That was the mistake.
The first American I ever met was not a person. It was a movie. White teeth. A car the size of a boat. A girl who kissed a stranger because the music told her to.

Then the gum. You chewed in public like the world was a ballpark. You put your feet on the seat. You talked to the waiter like he was your cousin. In my notes that was not charm. That was a country with no belt.
Jazz. You called it music. I called it a room that could not sit down. Hollywood. You called it art. I called it a factory that sold feelings by the pound, with a ticket stub.
You clapped when the picture ended, and you clapped when the plane landed, and you clapped when a man in a hat told you you were free. You clapped so much I thought you had no other language.
I wrote down the smile. You smiled at cameras. At shop windows. At people who had just taken your money. A smile was a tell. You wanted to be liked more than you wanted to win.

I watched your movies the way a butcher watches a cow. The hero breaks the rules and gets a speech. The war ends because the music gets loud. I did not believe the movies. I believed that you did. That was useful. For a while.

By the time a real American walked into a real room, the cartoon was already sitting there, eating popcorn. You argued with the cartoon for twenty minutes. The cartoon was more consistent than you were. You called that personality.
Second folder. Thinner. Cost more. Not what you said. You said everything, into a microphone, into a crowd, into a joke. It was what you bought when you thought nobody was keeping score.

You would sell a principle for a cheaper ticket. You would sell a friend for a better deal, then post a sunset about loyalty. You would sell a secret to feel like the smartest man at a table of people who already knew.

Money was the lazy tool. Money showed up on paper. Ego did not. I led with a tour. A factory visit. A famous name who remembered your paper, or pretended to. You would trade a map for a good seat. I was only half joking. The half that was joking still took notes.
You thought you were a country. I thought you were a market that had learned to salute. Markets crash. Then they come back. Same product. New color. New slogan. Same hunger.

Here is the sentence I promised. The one I got wrong. I wrote: they will not come. They will stay home with the radio and the ice cream and the argument. Screenshot that. I already knew you would. I did not know I would be the fool in the margin.

Now the number. I respected the hardware. I will say that even now. Factories. Steel. A country that could pour a ship like other countries poured a statue. I said that in private. I was not lying. That should have worried me more than it did.

I did not respect the will. Hardware is a receipt. Will is a mood. I counted how long you argued with yourselves before anything got done. I had a number. Isolation. A speech. A committee. Then baseball.

The number was this. Longer than your protests. Shorter than your attention. You get loud. Then you get bored. Then you go home. A long hard job does not sell tickets. A football game does. I filed that under victory. File it under stupid.
I did not need you weak. Weak is messy. I needed you busy. Three crises. An election. A game on the radio. That is a giant on mute. I liked you on mute. Mute is how a store stays a store.

The soldier in my folder was not a coward. He was a boy who went home when the pictures got bad and the comments got mean. I planned around the pictures. I planned around the fact that your news still sold the gum. Yes. That gum again. You remember it. That was the point. Until it was not.

This is the page that should make you sit up. I thought I understood the ending because I had seen the movie. The hero shows up late. The hero makes a speech. The credits roll. I ran the world like I had already watched the ending. I had not.

A promise is not a promise. It is a mood that dies in November, next to the gym membership and the campaign song. I did not take your word. I took your calendar. Calendars do not fight. People do. I mixed those up.

How many months until your election. How many months until the circus with different hats. You picked a man with a radio voice. Then you argued about him until the argument became the weather. I waited for the weather to change you. Weather does not change a factory.

Then a Sunday nobody in my office had put on the calendar the way it deserved. Smoke on water. A flag on fire in a photograph. I did not gasp. Gasping is your hobby. I checked the time. I should have checked the steel.

You think I wanted you divided. That is cute. Division is the exhaust. The engine is your attention. I pointed it at your fights. You pointed it at me. I did not like that plot twist. I had not paid for that ticket.

I do not invent your fights. You publish them. You fund them. You put a donate button under them. A panel about America falling apart, with sandwiches. A famous person reading a war speech they could not find on a map an hour ago. The lighting was excellent. I took notes. The notes were wrong.

The choir was not secret. It had a tote bag and a microphone. We used to plant stories. Then we just handed the already-angry American a bigger room. He did the rest himself. That still works. It did not stop the ships.

You call it a marketplace of ideas. I called it a buffet. I did not cook. I showed up hungry while you fought about the spoons. The most valuable American was not a spy. Spies want money. This one wanted to be right in public, for free, and called it being real.

If you are waiting for a villain in a dark coat with a secret envelope, you have the wrong century. The envelope was a quote. The quote was yours. I did not even edit it. You wrote my jokes for me. Then you wrote my ending, and I did not like the handwriting.

Now the other American. The one I actually had to count. Not the cartoon. The cartoon is the movies, and the movies are for you. These ones were in the factories. In the yards. On a line that did not stop for a speech. Quiet is expensive. Quiet built a fleet.

They talked about freedom at lunch. At dinner the line still moved. One country votes. One country welds. Guess which number I should have kept. You already know. I learned it late. Late is a word that tastes like smoke.

I watched a senator's speech about staying out. I did not cheer. I filed it. Filing is not the same as winning. I have used the same pencil for three of your moods. It is not even a nice pencil. The pencil outlived the mood. The mood did not outlive the ships.

Your politics have a cleaner word. Machine. Machines jam. They make the same noise before they fail. You film the noise and argue about who made it. Fifty percent plus one. A coin flip with fireworks. I bet on the jam. The machine spat out a war anyway.

A country staring at itself cannot stare across an ocean. That was my favorite line. I said it until I believed it. Then you stared at a poster, and a factory, and a boy with a bag, and the ocean got smaller. I do not like when a joke becomes a map.

You will find this out in a documentary. Sad piano. Three years later. Eating popcorn. Yes. That popcorn. I told you I would bring it back. The movie version has a speech. The real version has a list. I am on the list. You like lists. You put them on shirts.

The machine is not evil. Evil is a movie word. You like movie words. The machine is late, loud, and then suddenly on time. That is the worst thing I can say about an enemy. Congratulations. You earned it. I did not mean it as a gift.

A new American walks on a stage and talks about never again, and a line he will not cross this time. He swears. On a brand. I do not cheer. Panic is not cardio when the panic is mine. I open the same folder. The cartoon is still in it. The gum. The soldier who goes home. And then the page I circled until the paper tore: they came anyway.

The headings have not moved. Only the photographs. You age. The file does not. That should offend you more than I do. I do not need you worse. I needed you you: loud, rich, late, sure that history was a sequel and you still had the best explosions. I was right about the explosions. I was wrong about the ending.

You will ask if I was right. Of course. You love a verdict. You will fight in the comments. Monster or prophet. I predicted that too. Last page. Under the gum wrapper. The prophet thing is a trap. Do not give it to me. Give it to the factory.

Someone is writing a speech about how this time is different. That sentence is older than your last three slogans. In a cold room, a man like me sharpens a pencil. It is not dramatic. It is maintenance. The cycle does not continue because I was a genius. Genius is a compliment you give so you do not have to think.

It continues because you are familiar. And familiarity, my American friends, is the most expensive thing you give away for free. I bought it. I paid later. Send this to someone who thinks the cartoon is the whole country. They will not thank you. The file will.
